M (Top) U.S. Geological Survey (USGS) intern Dakota Sievers shares the results of her summer
research project with community members. Dakota's project evaluated the geochemical

semantic_text: M (Top) U.S. Geological Survey (USGS) intern Dakota Sievers shares the results of her summer research project with community members. plain_text:
(Bottom left) USGS intern Dakota Sievers conducts fieldwork at Herring River as part of her
summer research project. This portion of the wetland was restricted from tidal flow more than
100 years ago, but seawater was reintroduced in 2020 when a dune was breached during a
winter storm. Now the wetland floods regularly, and the ecosystem is changing rapidly.
semantic_text: (Bottom left) USGS intern Dakota Sievers conducts fieldwork at Herring River as part of her summer research project. This portion of the wetland was restricted from tidal flow more than 100 years ago, but seawater was reintroduced in 2020 when a dune was breached during a winter storm. Now the wetland floods regularly, and the ecosystem is changing rapidly.

plain_text:
(Bottom right) USGS and Partnership Education Program intern Amari Johnson collects
porewater samples from Marsh Island, a marsh that was recently constructed in Fairhaven,
Massachusetts. Amari studied the exchange of water between the adjacent harbor and the
new marsh. The marsh was intentionally built at an elevation high in the tidal frame, to provide
habitat for species such as the salt marsh sparrow. Evaluating the hydrology and chemistry of
the new marsh is important for managers as they track vegetation growth and habitat.
semantic_text: (Bottom right) USGS and Partnership Education Program intern Amari Johnson collects porewater samples from Marsh Island, a marsh that was recently constructed in Fairhaven, Massachusetts. Amari studied the exchange of water between the adjacent harbor and the new marsh. The marsh was intentionally built at an elevation high in the tidal frame, to provide habitat for species such as the salt marsh sparrow. Evaluating the hydrology and chemistry of the new marsh is important for managers as they track vegetation growth and habitat.
